who: David Mark Griffiths, historian of eighteenth-century Russia at UNC Chapel Hill, PhD Cornell.

evidence.says: Identifies David Mark Griffiths as a Cornell PhD who spent almost his entire academic career at UNC Chapel Hill, supervised doctoral dissertations, and specialized in Catherine II.
The candidate authority identifies David N. Griffiths, also David Nigel Griffiths, librarian of Lincoln Cathedral and author of The Bibliography of the Book of Common Prayer.
The other candidate authority has the authorized name David B. Griffiths and cites A Critical Bibliography of Writings on Judaism.

notes: Neither candidate is David Mark Griffiths: p-122002 is David Nigel Griffiths; p-44642 resolves to David B. Griffiths despite its abbreviated supplied label.

who: Robert E. Sullivan, intellectual historian at Notre Dame, PhD Harvard.

evidence.says: Notre Dame history professor with AM and PhD degrees from Harvard; author of John Toland and the Deist Controversy and Macaulay: The Tragedy of Power.
Authority identifies Robert E. Sullivan through John Toland and the Deist Controversy and Higher Learning and Catholic Traditions, both also listed on the Notre Dame profile.
The other Robert E. Sullivan authority instead identifies Rob Sullivan, author of Geography Speaks.

notes: Matching works and Harvard doctorate identify p-73461. The similarly initialed p-147603 is a different author; the remaining candidates are Robert R. Sullivan at John Jay/CUNY and the author of Rats.

who: Eugene M. Tobin, historian of American social and political history, visiting faculty at Miami University before 1980, PhD Brandeis.

evidence.says: Tobin held a visiting appointment at Miami University, Ohio, before joining Hamilton in 1980; earned his PhD in the history of American civilization at Brandeis; later served as Hamilton president and a Mellon program officer.
Authority names Eugene M. Tobin, author of Organize or Perish; its Locus of Authority citation identifies him as a former Hamilton president and Mellon senior program officer.

notes: The authority and institutional biography identify the same historian. His pre-1980 Miami appointment fits the 1979 dissertation; the biography does not specify its exact dates.

who: Julian Gwyn, University of Ottawa historian of Canadian economic and naval history.

evidence.says: The authority for Julian Gwyn cites Excessive Expectations and identifies its author as professor emeritus of history at the University of Ottawa.
Contributor information identifies Julian Gwyn as a professor in the University of Ottawa history department.
Lists Julian Gwyn as author of Ashore and Afloat: The British Navy and the Halifax Naval Yard Before 1820, closely matching the student dissertation field.

notes: Candidate authority explicitly supplies the missing Ottawa affiliation, and his naval-history work agrees with Hubley’s field. Direct supervision was not independently documented.

who: Paula Clarke, McGill history professor and Isabel Harvey’s doctoral supervisor, PhD London.

evidence.says: Page 12 lists Isabel Harvey’s PhD, names Paula Clarke as supervisor, and gives the matching dissertation title on monastic identity and bodily practices in Italy.
Lists Paula Clarke as an associate professor in history with a PhD from London.
Identifies Paul T. Clarke, whose Harvard doctorate in African and African American Studies ran from 2016 to 2024; lists research on policing in South Africa.

notes: The candidate is Paul T. Clarke, a different scholar with a different doctoral institution, field, and career timeline.

who: Keith Neilson, historian of British foreign policy and Anglo-Russian relations at the Royal Military College of Canada, PhD Cambridge.

evidence.says: A 2010 event identifies Neilson as RMC history professor with thirty years there, a Cambridge PhD, and expertise in British foreign policy and Anglo-Russian relations.
Authority identifies Keith Neilson through Strategy and Supply; the citation explicitly places its author in the RMC history department.

notes: The candidate authority explicitly links him to the student’s institution; his appointment and Anglo-Russian field fit the 2012 dissertation.

who: Jennifer S. H. Brown, ethnohistorian at the University of Winnipeg with graduate supervision involving Manitoba.

evidence.says: Identifies Jennifer S. H. Brown and Susan Elaine Gray as coeditors, describes Gray as Brown’s student, and connects Gray’s doctoral research to Berens River and the resulting book I Will Fear No Evil.
Lists Brown’s Winnipeg history appointments from 1983 to 2011 and graduate supervision throughout that period, including PhD committees; also lists Manitoba graduate dissertation service from 1998.
Identifies Jennifer S. H. Brown as professor emeritus of history at the University of Winnipeg and author of Strangers in Blood.
The alternative authority identifies Jen Corrinne Brown, author of Trout Culture, with a Washington State PhD and a Texas A&M history affiliation.

notes: The student relationship and precise Berens River research identify p-694. The other candidate is Jen Corrinne Brown.

who: James E. Fraser, Scottish historian at the University of Guelph since 2015, PhD Edinburgh 2003.

evidence.says: Identifies James E. Fraser, Edinburgh PhD 2003, Guelph associate professor since 2015 and Scottish Studies Foundation Chair from 2015 to 2020.
The candidate authority identifies James W. Fraser as professor of history and education at New York University and author of By the People.

notes: The Edinburgh doctorate and Guelph appointment identify James E. Fraser. Candidate p-127576 is James W. Fraser at NYU, a different historian.
